keyVerseText: Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.
rootMeaning: The Greek adjective σαπρός (saprós) derives from the verb σήπω (sḗpō), which means 'to be corrupted' or 'to putrefy.' This root conveys the idea of decay and moral degradation, emphasizing a process of rotting or becoming worthless. Beyond the common English glosses like 'corrupt' or 'bad,' the root sense highlights both a literal and figurative decay, suggesting something that has lost its vitality and integrity, whether physically or morally.
usageInScripture: The word σαπρός appears eight times in the New Testament, commonly translated as 'corrupt' or 'a corrupt.' Its usage consistently describes something spoiled, rotten, or morally worthless, whether applied to trees, fruit, speech, or other objects. The range of translations, including 'the bad' and 'can a corrupt,' reflects a focus on the inherent defectiveness or impurity of the subject, revealing a strong metaphorical extension from physical rot to moral corruption.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding σαπρός as both literally rotten and morally corrupt deepens our grasp of biblical warnings against impurity and falsehood. It reminds believers that just as physical decay renders something useless, moral corruption renders a person or their actions spiritually unfruitful and displeasing to God. This word underscores the necessity of holiness and integrity in the Christian life, contrasting the decay of sin with the vitality of righteousness. It also points to the transformative power of Christ, who redeems what is corrupt and makes it good and fruitful.
keyVerseReflection: Matthew 7:17 states, 'Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.' Here, σαπρός characterizes a tree that is inherently rotten, producing worthless and harmful fruit. This vivid metaphor teaches that the moral condition of a person (the tree) determines the quality of their actions (the fruit). The word σαπρός intensifies the warning against spiritual decay and calls believers to bear fruit that reflects genuine goodness.
